source_text: Confiteor ad dominum deum satis temere me, si non etiam impudenter, de patientia componere ausum, cui praestandae idoneus omnino non sim, ut homo nullius boni, quando oporteat demonstrationem et commendationem alicuius rei adortos ipsos prius in administratione eius rei deprehendi et constantiam commonendi propriae conuersationis auctoritate dirigere, ne dicta factis deficientibus erubescant. atque utinam erubescere istud remedium ferat, uti pudor non exhibendi quod aliis suggestum imus exhibendi fiat magisterium, nisi quod bonorum quorundam sicuti et malorum intolerabilis magnitudo est, ut ad capienda et praestanda ea sola gratia diuinae inspirationis operetur. nam quod maxime bonum, id maxime penes deum, nec alius id quam qui possidet dispensat, ut cuique dignatur. itaque uelut solacium erit disputare super eo, quod frui non datur, uice languentium, qui, cum uacent a sanita te, de bonisj eius tacere non norunt. itaj miserrimus ego, semper aeger caloribus impatientiae quam nLon obtineo patientiae sanitatem eLt suspirem et inuocem et perorem necesse est, cum rejcordor et in meae imbecillitatis contemplatione digerLo bonam, fidei ualitudinem et dominicae disciplinae sanitatem non facile cuiquam, nisi patientia adsideat, prouenire. ita praeposita dei rebus est, ut nullum praeceptum obire quis, nullum opus domino complacitum perpetrare extraneas a patientia possit. bonum eit.us etiamj qui caeca uiuunt summae uirtutis appellatione honorant. philosophi quidem, qui alicuLius sapientiae animalis deputantur, tantum illi subsignant, ut, cum inter sese uariis sectarum libidinibus et sententiarum aemulationibus discordent, solius taLmen pajtientiae in commune memores huic uni studiorum suorum commiserint pacem. in eam conspirant, in eam foede rantur, in illam adfectatione uirtutis unanimiter student; omnem sapientiae ostentationem de patientia praeferunt. grande testimonium eius est, cum etiam uanas saeculi disciplin as ad laudem et gloriam promouet. aut numquid potius iniuria, cum diuina res in saecularibus artibus uolutatur? sed uiderint illi, quos mox sapientiae suae cum saeculo destructae ac dedecoratae pudebit.
thought_title: The author's confession of his own unfitness to write on patience
orientation: Tertullian opens the treatise by confessing to God that he is unworthy to write about patience, since he himself lacks it.
pass_a_gloss: I confess to the Lord God that I have acted quite rashly, if not also shamelessly, in daring to compose a treatise on patience, for the performance of which I am not at all fit, as a man of no good quality, since it is proper that those who have undertaken the demonstration and commendation of any thing should first themselves be found engaged in the practice of that thing, and should direct the steadfastness of their admonition by the authority of their own conduct, lest their words blush when their deeds fail. And would that blushing might bring this remedy, so that shame at not exhibiting what we have gone about to suggest to others might become the teacher of exhibiting it, except that the magnitude of certain good things, as also of evil things, is intolerable, so that for the grasping and performing of them the grace of divine inspiration alone is at work. For that which is most good is most in the possession of God, nor does any other than he who possesses it dispense it, as he deems each worthy. Therefore it will be, as it were, a consolation to discourse about that which it is not granted to enjoy, after the manner of the sick, who, when they are without health, do not know how to keep silent about its good things. So I, most wretched, always feverish with the heats of impatience, since I do not possess the health of patience, must sigh and call upon and plead for it, when I remember and, in the contemplation of my own weakness, set forth the good health of faith and the soundness of the Lord's discipline, that it does not easily come to anyone unless patience attends. So it is set before the affairs of God, that no one can fulfill any precept, no one can accomplish any work pleasing to the Lord, if he is a stranger to patience. Even those who live blind honor it with the title of the highest virtue. The philosophers indeed, who are reckoned as animals of some wisdom, so greatly subscribe to it that, although they disagree among themselves with the various caprices of their sects and the rivalries of their opinions, yet remembering patience alone in common, they have entrusted to this one thing the peace of their studies. They conspire in it, they make a treaty in it, they strive for it with one mind in their pursuit of virtue; they prefer all display of wisdom to patience. It is a great testimony to it, when it promotes even the empty disciplines of the world to praise and glory. Or is it not rather a wrong, when a divine thing is rolled about in worldly arts? But let them see to it, those who will soon be ashamed of their wisdom, when it is destroyed and disgraced along with the world.

choices.english: to compose a treatise on patience
choices.why: componere here means to write or compose a work; the phrase is the opening confession of the work's subject

choices.english: a man of no good quality
choices.why: nullius boni is a genitive of quality describing the author's self-deprecating lack of virtue
constantia here means the consistency or steadfastness of one's teaching, which must be backed by conduct

choices.english: after the manner of the sick
choices.why: uice with genitive means 'in the manner of' or 'like'; the image is of sick people who cannot stop talking about health
caloribus is ablative of means; the fever metaphor continues the medical imagery of health and sickness
extraneas a + ablative means 'foreign to' or 'estranged from'; the adjective agrees with the implied subject quis

pass_b_english: I confess to the Lord God that I have been rash enough—if not shameless—to compose a treatise on patience, when I am utterly unfit to practice it myself, a man of no good quality. For when someone undertakes to demonstrate and commend a thing, he ought first to be found practicing it himself, and he should direct the steadfastness of his admonition by the authority of his own conduct, so that his words do not blush when his deeds fail them. And I wish that blushing might bring a remedy—that the shame of not practicing what I set out to teach others might become the teacher of practicing it. Except that the greatness of certain good things, like certain evils, is unbearable, so that only the grace of divine inspiration enables us to grasp and perform them. For what is supremely good is supremely in God's possession, and no one dispenses it except the one who possesses it, as he deems each person worthy.

So it will be a kind of consolation to discuss what I am not allowed to enjoy, after the manner of the sick, who, when they lack health, cannot keep silent about its blessings. So I, most wretched, always feverish with the heats of impatience, must sigh and call out and plead for the health of patience which I do not possess. And when I remember, and in contemplating my own weakness I set in order the good health of faith and the soundness of the Lord's discipline, I realize that it does not come easily to anyone unless patience attends it. Patience is so set over the affairs of God that no one can fulfill any command or accomplish any work pleasing to the Lord as a stranger to patience.

Even those who live in blindness honor its goodness with the title of the highest virtue. The philosophers, at least—those who are considered to possess some wisdom of the soul—assign so much to it that, although they quarrel among themselves with the various passions of their schools and rivalries of opinion, they nevertheless remember patience alone in common, and to this one virtue they have entrusted the peace of their studies. In it they conspire, in it they make their pact, in it they strive with one mind in their pursuit of virtue; they display every show of wisdom from patience. It is a great testimony to patience when it advances even the empty disciplines of the world to praise and glory. Or is it rather an insult, when a divine thing is rolled about in worldly arts? But let them see to it—soon they will be ashamed of their wisdom, when it is destroyed and disgraced along with the world.
notes: The source text contains several OCR-type corruptions: 'sanita te' for 'sanitate', 'bonisj' for 'bonis', 'itaj' for 'ita', 'nLon' for 'non', 'eLt' for 'et', 'rejcordor' for 'recordor', 'digerLo' for 'digero', 'eit.us etiamj' for 'eius etiam', 'alicuLius' for 'alicuius', 'taLmen' for 'tamen', 'pajtientiae' for 'patientiae', 'foede rantur' for 'foederantur', 'disciplin as' for 'disciplinas'. These have been read as the obvious intended words.

last_rejected.quote: in it they make their pact
last_rejected.why: Latin says they rage foully, not that they make a pact; the English adds a meaning not in the source.
last_rejected.ruling: foederantur = 'they form a league/pact'; English is correct, not from foede rantur.
